detailed_findings.finding: The map n ↦ k = I(n-1) is correctly shown to be a bijection from {2,...,p-1} onto {1,...,p-2}, and the equivalence k ∈ S iff n + I(n) > p + 2 is derived correctly.
detailed_findings.location: First half of the proof, from the definition of A through the conclusion |S| = |A|

detailed_findings.finding: The pairing argument on B = {2,...,p-2} using n ↦ p-n is valid: I(p-n) = p-I(n), the sum transforms by s ↦ 2p-s, and the involution has no fixed points because p is odd.
detailed_findings.location: Middle counting argument introducing B and E

detailed_findings.finding: The exceptional set estimate is complete: c = p-2 and c = p+2 lead to impossible square congruences, while c = p-1, p, p+1 each give a nonzero quadratic over F_p and therefore at most two solutions modulo p.

reason: The proof is mathematically sound and complete for the stated residue class p ≡ 1 (mod 8). It gives a correct bijection between S and a set A defined by n + I(n) > p + 2, then counts A via the involution n ↦ p-n on B = {2,...,p-2}, isolating an exceptional set E where the paired sums lie in [p-2,p+2]. The bound |E| ≤ 6 is justified by reducing each possible sum value to a quadratic congruence, with two impossible square cases and three degree-2 cases having at most two roots each over the field F_p. The final arithmetic comparison with floor(p/4) is correct when p = 8m+1, m ≥ 2.
